refuted_candidates.failure_scenario: An operator invokes cancel(execution, 'tenant offboarded') on the Temporal adapter; after the reason-bounds check passes, handle.cancel(reason=...) raises TypeError('cancel() got an unexpected keyword argument \'reason\'') on every invocation, so no cancellation request ever reaches Temporal and the durable workflow execution keeps running. The path has no test coverage (no cancel test in test_agent_runtime_temporal_integration.py or the conformance harness).
refuted_candidates.summary: TemporalDurableBackendAdapter.cancel calls `await handle.cancel(reason=reason)`, but temporalio's WorkflowHandle.cancel() accepts no `reason` parameter (only rpc_metadata/rpc_timeout; `reason` exists on terminate()), so the call raises TypeError.

verification_history.evidence: The claim that temporalio's WorkflowHandle.cancel() accepts no `reason` parameter is factually wrong for the SDK version this repo requires. pyproject.toml line 15 pins `temporal = ["temporalio>=1.31"]`, and in temporalio 1.31.0 (wheel temporalio-1.31.0-cp310-abi3, temporalio/client/_workflow.py line 319) the signature is: `async def cancel(self, *, reason: str = "", rpc_metadata: Mapping[str, str | bytes] = {}, rpc_timeout: timedelta | None = None) -> None:` with docstring 'reason: Reason recorded with the cancellation request. Available inside the workflow via temporalio.workflow.cancellation_reason'. Therefore `await handle.cancel(reason=reason)` at durability_temporal_coordination.py:331 is a valid keyword call and raises no TypeError under any install satisfying the declared `>=1.31` constraint; the `reason`-only-on-terminate() behavior the candidate describes belongs to older SDK versions the pin excludes. (The secondary observation that cancel has no test coverage is accurate but does not establish the claimed defect.)

release_blockers.failure_scenario: A Product Gateway submits an authorized external event, the response is lost to a network failure, and it retries prepare_ingress with the exact same ExternalEventIngressRequest and evidence but a fresh claim_at_utc (current time). The rebuilt record differs only in recorded_at_utc, so `existing != record` and the call raises ValueError 'external-event ingress idempotency conflict'; the retry path can never claim the wait even though apply() is written to be retry-safe, permanently stalling the waiting workflow transition for that request.
release_blockers.summary: prepare_ingress bakes the caller-supplied claim_at_utc into the ingress record (recorded_at_utc, hashed into ingress_record_sha256) and then requires full equality with the stored record for idempotent replay, so any retry of the identical request at a later timestamp raises instead of returning the committed record. [same root cause also at: src/agent_runtime/execution/execution_authorization_coordination.py:500]

release_blockers.summary: prepare_ingress rejects any requested event whose unique workflow edge is terminal (target_node_id is None), so an authorized external decision can never complete a waiting execution, even though project_workflow_release_graph supports terminal transitions via the 'completed' control state.

release_blockers.failure_scenario: A host submits RuntimeWorkflowStartRequest (or RuntimeCancellationRequest / RuntimeExecutionView) with recorded_at_utc="2026-08-08T12:00:00+05:30"; validation passes and the value is durably embedded in immutable start-request payloads, receipts, and canonical hashes even though the field contract and every other record in the system require Z-suffixed UTC. verified_findings.failure_scenario: A host implements the exported DurableWorkflowCursor protocol and validates incoming events with the facade type (`type(event) is agent_runtime.ExternalEvent`): every event the exported DurableExecutionCoordinator constructs in drive() is the un-exported topology ExternalEvent, so the check rejects it and every workflow drive fails after the first Module dispatch; conversely a caller constructing agent_runtime.ExternalEvent to call signal() gets a TypeError because its fields (event_ref, ingress_request_ref, event_sha256, expected_domain_state, ...) do not match the signal contract, and there is no public import path for the correct type.
verified_findings.summary: The package facade exports DurableWorkflowCursor and DurableExecutionCoordinator but binds the name ExternalEvent to the ingress-record type from execution_event_ingestion, while the exported cursor protocol's signal() consumes durability_topology_definition.ExternalEvent (event_id/expected_state/target_state/evidence_ref), which is exported nowhere publicly (contracts.__init__ exports yet a third ExternalEvent from registry_workflow_definition).

ExternalEvent, ...)' with 'ExternalEvent' in __all__ (line 171), while lines 73-79 export 'DurableExecutionCoordinator' and 'DurableWorkflowCursor'. verification_history.evidence: src/agent_runtime/contracts/execution_host_definition.py:21-24 reads `from ..execution.execution_event_ingestion import (ExternalEventAcknowledgement, ExternalEventIngressRequest,)` — a contracts module importing from the execution implementation package. Runtime demonstration: `import agent_runtime.contracts.execution_host_definition` alone loads agent_runtime.execution plus all seven execution modules (execution_authorization_coordination, execution_event_ingestion, execution_module_invocation, etc.) and six agent_runtime.registry modules (including registry_release_registration, reached via execution_event_ingestion.py:38 `from ..registry.registry_release_registration import RuntimeReleaseRegistry`). So any import-time failure in those implementation packages breaks contracts-only consumers exactly as claimed. The protocol signature claim is also verified: execution_host_definition.py:317-320 declares `async def submit_external_event(self, request: ExternalEventIngressRequest,) -> ExternalEventAcknowledgement:`, and both types' `__module__` is `agent_runtime.execution.execution_event_ingestion` — implementation-package types defining the contract surface.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: A host submits RuntimeWorkflowStartRequest with recorded_at_utc="2026-01-01T00:00:00+05:00"; this validator accepts it (any offset passes, line 36 is a no-op), the request is admitted and copied into Temporal start payloads, and the same execution later fails deep inside ledger commit where ledger _validate_utc requires a zero offset — a late, hard-to-diagnose mid-execution failure instead of a boundary rejection. Using the existing validate_utc_timestamp removes both the duplicate and the drift.
verified_findings.summary: _validate_utc re-implements the shared validate_utc_timestamp helper (already imported from registry_contract_validation) with weaker semantics that accept non-UTC offsets, plus a dead `parsed.astimezone(timezone.utc)` statement whose result is discarded

verification_history.evidence: execution_host_definition.py:34 reads `if parsed.tzinfo is None or parsed.utcoffset() is None:` — it only requires that SOME offset exists, so recorded_at_utc="2026-01-01T00:00:00+05:00" passes RuntimeWorkflowStartRequest.validate() (line 132: `_validate_utc("recorded_at_utc", self.recorded_at_utc)`); verified by executing the validator logic: the host validator accepts +05:00. Line 36 `parsed.astimezone(timezone.utc)` is a dead statement — astimezone returns a new datetime that is never assigned or checked (verified: original stays 2026-01-01T00:00:00+05:00). The shared helper the module bypasses, registry_contract_validation.validate_utc_timestamp (lines 148-158), rejects the same value twice over: line 151 `if type(value) is not str or not value.endswith("Z")` and line 157 `if parsed.utcoffset() is None or parsed.utcoffset().total_seconds() != 0`; execution_host_definition.py lines 14-20 already import five other validators from that exact module (validate_bool, validate_id, validate_opaque_ref, validate_sha256, validate_string_tuple), so the duplicate is gratuitous. The drift is real and cross-layer: ledger_record_definition.py:116 `if parsed.tzinfo is None or parsed.utcoffset() != timedelta(0): raise ValueError(f"{label} must be UTC")` requires a zero offset, as do registry_release_definition.py:60-68 and every validate_utc_timestamp call site — the host boundary is the only layer accepting non-UTC offsets into fields named *_utc. The admitted request is indeed copied into Temporal start payloads: durability_temporal_coordination.py:422 `execution_payload = request.as_dict()` feeds `client.start_workflow(...)` (lines 434-436) and is reconstructed in-workflow at line 93 via `RuntimeWorkflowStartRequest.from_dict(request_payload)`. One caveat on the scenario's tail: no code inside this repo literally copies request.recorded_at_utc into a ledger record, so the exact "fails deep inside ledger commit" step depends on host wiring that carries the boundary timestamp forward — but the core defect (boundary validator weaker than every downstream *_utc validator, plus the no-op line 36) is directly constructible from the quoted lines.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: A host submits RuntimeWorkflowStartRequest (or RuntimeCancellationRequest / RuntimeExecutionView) with recorded_at_utc="2026-08-08T12:00:00+05:30"; validation passes and the value is durably embedded in immutable start-request payloads, receipts, and canonical hashes even though the field contract and every other record in the system require Z-suffixed UTC. Consumers that assume the uniform grammar break: lexicographic ordering of recorded_at_utc across records no longer matches chronological order, and any component that later revalidates the copied value with validate_utc_timestamp rejects it ("UTC timestamp ending in Z required"), failing an execution that was already admitted.
verified_findings.summary: _validate_utc ends with `parsed.astimezone(timezone.utc)` whose return value is discarded — a no-op statement — so unlike validate_utc_timestamp used by every other Runtime contract (which requires a trailing Z and a zero offset), the product-host boundary accepts timestamps with any non-UTC offset.

verification_history.evidence: src/agent_runtime/contracts/execution_host_definition.py:36 is `parsed.astimezone(timezone.utc)` — the return value is discarded and datetime.astimezone() never raises for an aware datetime, so it is a no-op; the only offset check is line 34 `if parsed.tzinfo is None or parsed.utcoffset() is None`, which accepts any offset. Executed proof: `_validate_utc('recorded_at_utc', '2026-08-08T12:00:00+05:30')` passes, while the shared validator rejects the identical value (`registry_contract_validation.py:151` `if type(value) is not str or not value.endswith("Z"): raise ValueError(f"invalid {label}: UTC timestamp ending in Z required")` and line 157 zero-offset check). Every other Runtime contract enforces zero offset: ledger_lineage/execution_operation/execution_authorization import validate_utc_timestamp; registry_release_definition.py:60-68 is a verbatim strict copy; ledger_record_definition.py:111-117 requires `parsed.utcoffset() != timedelta(0)` to fail. The admitted value is durably serialized: durability_temporal_coordination.py:422 `execution_payload = request.as_dict()` and line 93 `RuntimeWorkflowStartRequest.from_dict(request_payload)` round-trip the start request (including recorded_at_utc) as backend workflow input, and any strict revalidation of the copied value fails with "UTC timestamp ending in Z required", exactly as the candidate describes.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: run_module builds ModuleAttemptRecord with period_start from the attempt-start record and period_end from a later clock() call; with an injected non-monotonic clock (test/evaluation callers may pass any Callable[[], str]) or host clock skew, an attempt whose period_end_at_utc precedes period_start_at_utc validates and commits to the immutable ledger, producing negative-duration lineage that downstream duration/usage projections silently consume, whereas the legacy record type rejected the same record.
verified_findings.summary: ModuleAttemptRecord.validate — the target-model rewrite of the legacy WorkflowAttemptRecord — validates period_start_at_utc, period_end_at_utc, and recorded_at_utc only individually and dropped the legacy record's interval guard (ledger_record_definition.py:530-537 raises when period_end precedes period_start).

verification_history.evidence: ModuleAttemptRecord.validate (ledger_lineage_definition.py:245-250) checks the interval fields only individually — `for label, value in (("period_start_at_utc", ...), ("period_end_at_utc", ...), ("recorded_at_utc", ...)): validate_utc_timestamp(label, value)` — and the rest of the method (lines 228-278) contains no end-vs-start comparison; validate_utc_timestamp (registry_contract_validation.py:148-158) is single-field format validation only. The legacy WorkflowAttemptRecord.validate has exactly the guard the candidate cites (ledger_record_definition.py:536-537): `if period_end < period_start: raise ValueError("Attempt period_end_at_utc precedes period_start_at_utc")`. The trigger is constructible: run_module accepts an injectable clock (execution_module_invocation.py:117 `clock: Callable[[], str] = _utc_now`); `started_at = clock()` (line 156) becomes ModuleAttemptStartedRecord.recorded_at_utc (line 225) and then `period_start_at_utc=attempt_start.recorded_at_utc` (lines 283/324), while a later `ended_at = clock()` (lines 274/294) becomes `period_end_at_utc=ended_at` (lines 284/325); the default _utc_now is non-monotonic wall clock `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` (line 81). No guard exists elsewhere on this path: InMemoryModuleExecutionLedger.commit_attempt (ledger_lineage_recording.py:98-106) calls only `attempt.validate()` before storing, and the persistence checks at ledger_record_persistence.py:703-706 apply to the legacy WorkflowAttemptRecord/WorkflowAttemptStartedRecord flow (they reference dispatch_id, trace_id, and start.deadline_at(), fields absent from the module lineage types). So a clock returning e.g. "2026-01-01T00:00:10.000000Z" then "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z" produces an attempt with period_end_at_utc < period_start_at_utc that validates and commits to the immutable ledger, where the legacy record type raised ValueError. Minor caveat not affecting the verdict: no shipped projection currently reads ModuleAttemptRecord.period_* (grep shows only the construction site and legacy-type consumers), so the "downstream projections consume" clause is prospective, but the negative-duration record is returned in ModuleRunResult and preserved as an immutable record.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Two parallel validator families guard the same grammar; a tightening applied to the shared module (e.g. a new secret marker) silently does not apply to ledger records, so a ref that one boundary rejects is committed to the authoritative ledger by the other — the drift already exists for UTC handling (ledger accepts '+00:00' suffix, shared helper requires trailing 'Z').
verified_findings.summary: Private _validate_id/_validate_sha/_validate_ref/_validate_utc and the _ID/_SHA256/_OPAQUE_REF/_SECRET_MARKERS constants re-implement validate_id/validate_sha256/validate_opaque_ref/validate_utc_timestamp and the identical patterns already exported by contracts/registry_contract_validation.py

verification_history.evidence: Duplication is exact: ledger_record_definition.py:25-28 defines `_ID = re.compile(r"^[a-z][a-z0-9_.-]{2,159}$")`, `_SHA256 = re.compile(r"^[0-9a-f]{64}$")`, `_OPAQUE_REF = re.compile(r"^[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]{0,63}:[^\s]{1,447}$")`, `_SECRET_MARKERS = ("password=", "token=", "secret=", "apikey=", "api_key=")` — byte-identical to registry_contract_validation.py:17-21 (`ID_PATTERN`, `SHA256_PATTERN`, `OPAQUE_REF_PATTERN`, `SECRET_MARKERS`), and `_validate_id`/`_validate_sha`/`_validate_ref` (lines 86-101) mirror the exported `validate_id`/`validate_sha256`/`validate_opaque_ref`. ledger_record_definition.py imports nothing from registry_contract_validation (its only intra-package imports, lines 21-22, are `.ledger_lineage_definition` and `.registry_workflow_definition`), while 14 other modules — including sibling `contracts/ledger_lineage_definition.py:16` and `execution/execution_authorization_coordination.py:22` (`validate_utc_timestamp`) — use the shared family, so the two parallel validator families coexist across live boundaries. The claimed UTC drift is real and demonstrated by execution: `_validate_utc` (line 113: `datetime.fromisoformat(str(value).replace("Z", "+00:00"))`) ACCEPTS '2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00', while shared `validate_utc_timestamp` (line 151: `if type(value) is not str or not value.endswith("Z")`) REJECTS the identical string with 'invalid recorded_at_utc: UTC timestamp ending in Z required'. So a `recorded_at_utc` that the shared boundary rejects validates cleanly in a ledger record (e.g. WorkflowModuleRunRecord.validate -> _validate_utc, line 260), and any future tightening of the shared module (e.g. a new SECRET_MARKERS entry) silently would not apply to ledger refs — exactly the stated failure scenario. A secondary drift compounds it: the ledger validators coerce via `str(value)` (line 87) where the shared ones require `type(value) is str` (registry_contract_validation.py:48).

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Each record validation parses the same timestamp strings twice (validate + use), and lease-expiry checks parse four strings per admission record on every validate() call in the commit path; wasted parsing multiplies with the 3-5x validation cascade per ledger commit. A parse-once helper that returns the datetime removes the redundancy.
verified_findings.summary: _validate_utc parses timestamps with datetime.fromisoformat but every consumer that needs the value (deadline_at, expires_at, lease checks at lines 482, 530-535, 962-967, 1047-1052, 1244) re-parses the identical string again after validate() already parsed it

verification_history.evidence: _validate_utc parses and discards: line 113 `parsed = datetime.fromisoformat(str(value).replace("Z", "+00:00"))` (returns None; `parsed` used only for the UTC check at 116). Every consumer re-parses the same string after validate() already parsed it: line 482 `start = datetime.fromisoformat(self.recorded_at_utc.replace("Z", "+00:00"))` runs right after `self.validate()` (481) which parsed recorded_at_utc at 476; lines 530-535 re-parse period_start_at_utc/period_end_at_utc just parsed by _validate_utc at 527-528; lines 962-966 and 1047-1051 re-parse both lease timestamps parsed at 960-961/1045-1046 (4 fromisoformat executions per admission-record validate); line 1244 re-parses recorded_at_utc parsed at 1238 via validate() at 1243. The claimed validation cascade is also real: RuntimeRecordBatch.as_dict() (2686-2694) calls self.validate() at 2689 — which runs runtime_record_as_dict(record) per record at 2678 — then runtime_record_as_dict again at 2693, and transaction_sha256 (2700) calls as_dict() on top; the commit path (ledger_record_persistence.py 204-205 `claim.validate(); batch.validate()` then commit(batch.as_record_batch()) validating again at 318/331) multiplies per-record parses 3-5x per ledger commit. Efficiency-only redundancy, but the claim is factually accurate with an always-on trigger.

_validate_utc (lines 111-117) parses `parsed = datetime.fromisoformat(str(value).replace("Z", "+00:00"))`, uses it only for the tz check, and returns None — the datetime is discarded. Every cited consumer then re-parses the identical string: deadline_at() calls self.validate() at line 481 (which ran `_validate_utc("recorded_at_utc", ...)` at 476) then line 482 re-parses `start = datetime.fromisoformat(self.recorded_at_utc.replace("Z", "+00:00"))`; WorkflowAttemptRecord.validate() runs _validate_utc on period_start_at_utc/period_end_at_utc at 527-528 then re-parses both at 530-535 for the interval check; ExecutionStartAdmissionRecord.validate() parses both timestamps via _validate_utc at 960-961 then re-parses both at 962-966 in the lease-expiry comparison (four fromisoformat calls for two strings per validate()); ModuleDispatchAdmissionRecord.validate() repeats the same pattern at 1045-1046 → 1047-1051; expires_at() calls self.validate() at 1243 (parse at 1238) then re-parses at 1244. The multiplier is real too: as_dict() re-runs validate() on every serialization, and commit paths validate again (ledger_record_persistence.py:204-205, 266-267; ledger_lineage_recording.py:64-69). Trigger is unconditional — every validate()/deadline_at()/expires_at() call performs the redundant parse.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Eighteen hand-copied implementations of the same integrity mechanism must stay in lockstep; a record added with a subtly different pop-field or ordering silently produces hashes that fail cross-validation, and any improvement (e.g. avoiding the double hash in build+validate) requires 18 coordinated edits. A single content_addressed_build(cls, hash_field, fields) helper or mixin does the same job.
verified_findings.summary: The content-addressing pattern (_identity_payload popping the hash field + build() constructing a provisional record with '0'*64 then rebuilding with sha256_json) is copy-pasted 13 times in this file and 5 more times as _payload/build in execution_event_ingestion.py

verification_history.evidence: Counts are exact. ledger_record_definition.py contains exactly 13 `def _identity_payload` definitions (lines 837, 914, 996, 1077, 1582, 1883, 1941, 2054, 2130, 2217, 2294, 2359, 2481), each an asdict+pop of its hash field — e.g. lines 837-840: `payload = asdict(self); payload.pop("binding_sha256"); return payload` — and each paired with a copy-pasted build(), e.g. lines 846-849: `provisional = cls(**fields, binding_sha256="0" * 64)` then `binding_sha256=sha256_json(provisional._identity_payload())`; the same provisional-'0'*64 construction repeats at lines 923, 1005, 1086, 1591, 1892, 1950, 2063, 2139, 2226, 2303, 2368, 2509. execution_event_ingestion.py contains exactly 5 more as `_payload`/`build` (lines 104, 159, 308, 403, 457 with builds at 128-137, 202-208, 379-385, 425-431, 523-529), e.g. line 131: `provisional = cls(**fields, snapshot_sha256="0" * 64)` / line 134: `snapshot_sha256=_canonical_sha256(provisional._payload())` — and `_canonical_sha256` (lines 41-48) is byte-identical canonicalization to the ledger's `sha256_json` (`json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))` + sha256), so all 18 are the same integrity mechanism. The lockstep/cross-validation risk is real: validate() re-derives the hash from the payload at line 885 (`if self.binding_sha256 != sha256_json(self._identity_payload()):`) and line 124 (`if self.snapshot_sha256 != _canonical_sha256(self._payload()):`), so a copy with a divergent pop-field silently hashes different content and fails that check. The claimed double hash also exists: `ExecutionSnapshotToken.build` computes the hash (line 134) then calls `record.validate()` (line 136) which recomputes it (line 124). The proposed single helper/mixin is viable since every build() already dispatches through `provisional._payload()`/`_identity_payload()` as an overridable hook (the only non-uniform bodies — EvaluationSet lines 2481-2494 and the nested event payloads at 403/457 — are per-class hook overrides). If anything the finding undercounts: the same pattern also appears 8x in execution_authorization_definition.py, 6x in execution_operation_definition.py, and 8x in registry_release_definition.py.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: One finalize_attempt call validates and canonical-JSON-serializes every record in the batch 3-5 times (store validates the batch, as_record_batch revalidates and rehashes the output bundle, commit() validates again and transaction_sha256 serializes once more) — the per-attempt commit path does several times the necessary hashing work. Serializing once and deriving both the validity check and the transaction hash from that single pass does the same job.
verified_findings.summary: RuntimeRecordBatch.as_dict validates every record via runtime_record_as_dict inside self.validate(), then serializes each record again in the comprehension; transaction_sha256 re-invokes as_dict, and AttemptFinalizationBatch.validate/as_record_batch each recompute _canonical_output_bundle (lines 3020, 3026)

verification_history.evidence: All three sub-claims are literal code, and the 3-5x multiplier is reproducible on every finalize_attempt call. (a) RuntimeRecordBatch.as_dict (ledger_record_definition.py:2686-2694) runs `self.validate()` at line 2689 — validate's loop at line 2678 calls `runtime_record_as_dict(record)`, which fully serializes each record (`return {"record_type": ..., "record": as_dict_method()}`, line 2659) and discards the result — then the comprehension at line 2693 (`"records": [runtime_record_as_dict(record) for record in self.records]`) serializes every record a second time. (b) transaction_sha256 (line 2697-2700) is a plain @property, not cached_property: `return sha256_json(self.as_dict())`, so it re-runs the whole double pass. (c) AttemptFinalizationBatch.validate ends with `self._canonical_output_bundle()` at line 3020 (result discarded), and as_record_batch calls `self.validate()` at 3025 then `output_bundle = self._canonical_output_bundle()` at 3026 — and _canonical_output_bundle does real hash work each time (`bundle_sha256 = attempt_output_bundle_sha256(outputs)`, line 2947, which is sha256 over canonical JSON per lines 64-76/48-51). The claimed finalize_attempt scenario is exact: ledger_record_persistence.py:205 `batch.validate()` (child records serialized pass 1, bundle hash #1), :245 `self.commit(batch.as_record_batch())` where as_record_batch revalidates (pass 2, bundle hash #2) and rebuilds the bundle (hash #3), then commit() at :354 `batch.validate()` (pass 3, all batch records) and :355 `batch.transaction_sha256` → as_dict → validate (pass 4) + comprehension (pass 5). Child records: 5 canonical-JSON serializations; terminal_attempt/output_bundle/invocation_commit: 3; bundle hash: 3 computations. `grep cached_property|lru_cache|functools` over both files returns nothing, so no memoization guards any of it. Only one pass's output is ever used.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Pure duplicate of an available shared helper; any future fix to timestamp validation (e.g. rejecting year-zero or leap-second strings) must be discovered and applied twice, and release records will accept timestamps the rest of the transport layer rejects when the copies diverge.

verified_findings.summary: _validate_snapshot re-runs graph.validate() (full canonical-JSON hash of the immutable projection) and execution.validate() on every dispatch iteration of drive(), although both objects were validated once at drive() entry and never change

verification_history.evidence: durability_workflow_coordination.py lines 332-334: `_validate_snapshot` runs `snapshot.validate()` / `graph.validate()` / `execution.validate()`, and it is called at line 240 inside `for dispatch_count in range(1, max_dispatches + 1):` (line 197, default `max_dispatches: int = 100` at line 168) after every `signal`. The cost claim is accurate: `WorkflowGraphProjection.validate()` recomputes the full canonical-JSON hash every call — `if self.graph_sha256 != self.computed_sha256(): raise ValueError(...)` (durability_topology_definition.py lines 782-783), where `computed_sha256` is `_canonical_hash(self._identity_payload())` doing `json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True, ...)` + `sha256` over all states (lines 126-133, 734-737) with no caching. Trigger: any drive() call executing multiple dispatch iterations — the normal path. Validating graph/execution once before the loop gives identical protection; the meaningful per-iteration cross-check `snapshot.graph_sha256 != graph.graph_sha256` (line 344) needs no re-hash of the unchanged frozen graph.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Two threads (e.g. two concurrent dispatches of the same execution through ExecutionAuthorizationController) call commit_binding with different bindings for the same workflow_execution_id: both read _binding_ref_by_execution before either writes, both pass the conflict check, and the second silently overwrites the first — each caller proceeds believing its own binding is the committed one, defeating the "duplicate-safe" ledger guarantee; the same race lets commit_fence re-open a concurrently-FENCED binding.
verified_findings.summary: InMemoryExecutionAuthorizationLedger (and its sibling InMemoryAuthorizationLedger in execution_operation_authorization.py:60) performs check-then-insert duplicate/conflict detection (commit_binding, commit_fence, commit_intent, commit_observation) over plain dicts with no lock, while every other in-memory store in the package (InMemoryModuleExecutionLedger, InMemoryCellArtifactStore, InMemoryRuntimeExecutionRecordStore, RuntimeReleaseRegistry) guards the same pattern with an RLock.

verification_history.evidence: Mechanism verified line-by-line. InMemoryExecutionAuthorizationLedger.__init__ (execution_authorization_coordination.py:53-60) creates plain dicts with no lock, and commit_binding is unlocked check-then-insert: line 69 'existing_ref = self._binding_ref_by_execution.get(binding.workflow_execution_id)', line 72 'if existing_ref is not None:', line 80 'self._binding_ref_by_execution[binding.workflow_execution_id] = (binding.binding_ref)'. Two threads committing different bindings for one workflow_execution_id can both read None at line 69 before either writes line 80; both bypass line 75 "raise ValueError('Workflow Execution authorization binding conflict')" (their binding_refs differ, so the line 77 ref check also passes) and the last writer silently wins — each caller returns its own binding at line 83 believing it committed. commit_fence has the same race: the monotonic guard (lines 100-107, returning current when 'current.state is ExecutionAuthorizationFenceState.FENCED and fence.state is ...OPEN') reads _current_fence_ref_by_binding before the line 112 write 'self._current_fence_ref_by_binding[fence.binding_ref] = fence.fence_ref', so a concurrent OPEN commit that read the pre-FENCED current overwrites a just-committed FENCED fence, violating the docstring 'Commit a fence without reopening a previously fenced binding' (line 97). commit_intent (lines 130-137) and commit_observation (lines 203-208) repeat the pattern, as does sibling InMemoryAuthorizationLedger (execution_operation_authorization.py:65-67, commit_request 83-86, commit_result 94-97 — no lock). The comparative claim is accurate for all four named stores: InMemoryModuleExecutionLedger (ledger_lineage_recording.py:24, 'Thread-safe test ledger', 'self._lock = RLock()' at :28, 'with self._lock:' around the identical check-then-insert at :43/:70; its begin docstring even anticipates 'a result won by a concurrent identical caller'), InMemoryCellArtifactStore (execution_content_staging.py:56), InMemoryRuntimeExecutionRecordStore (ledger_record_persistence.py:143), and RuntimeReleaseRegistry (registry_release_registration.py:94 'self._registration_lock = RLock()'). Verdict is PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED because the trigger is environment-dependent: every in-repo usage of the two unlocked ledgers is a single-threaded test fixture (test_agent_runtime_execution_authorization.py:135, test_agent_runtime_authorization.py:170), so nothing in the repo actually drives them from two threads; the class is, however, exported as public API (src/agent_runtime/__init__.py:71) and its docstring at line 51 declares it 'for portable tests and host integration', making multi-threaded host use (e.g. a Temporal sync-activity thread pool) realistic. Confirmation would be any host path sharing one ledger instance across threads, or a two-thread stress test calling commit_binding with two different bindings for the same workflow_execution_id and observing both succeed where serial execution raises ValueError at line 75. (Minor overbreadth in the claim: InMemoryExternalEventIngress at execution_event_ingestion.py:576-583 is also unlocked, so 'every other in-memory store' is not literally exhaustive, but all four stores the candidate names are RLock-guarded as claimed.)

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Reproduced: a durable coordinator retries revalidate(binding_ref=..., observed_at_utc=T) after a transient failure (same observed timestamp, standard replay semantics). _commit_fence derives fence_id only from (binding_sha256, status_sha256, state) but builds the record with recorded_at_utc=self._clock(); InMemoryExecutionAuthorizationLedger.commit_fence compares full equality and raises ValueError('execution authorization fence ref conflict'). verified_findings.summary: Fence/binding records embed a fresh clock timestamp under a timestamp-free ref, so retrying revalidate() or bind_execution_context() with identical inputs raises a ref-conflict ValueError instead of returning the duplicate-safe result the ledger promises.

verification_history.evidence: Reproduced both legs by construction with the default clock. Refs are timestamp-free while records embed a fresh clock reading: _commit_fence derives `fence_id = _stable_id("execution_authorization_fence", binding.binding_sha256, status.status_sha256, state.value,)` (execution_authorization_coordination.py:507-512) yet builds the fence with `recorded_at_utc=self._clock(),` (line 522); bind_execution_context derives binding_id from (workflow_execution_id, context_sha256, execution_input_package_sha256) (lines 286-291) yet sets `recorded_at_utc=self._clock(),` (line 308); default clock is live: `clock: Callable[[], str] = _utc_now` (line 221). `recorded_at_utc` participates in dataclass equality and in fence_sha256/binding_sha256 (execution_authorization_definition.py lines 393/406 and 319/322-327), so a retried record is unequal to the committed one under the same ref, and the ledger raises: `if existing != binding: raise ValueError("Workflow Execution authorization binding conflict")` (lines 74-75) and `if existing is not None and existing != fence: raise ValueError("execution authorization fence ref conflict")` (lines 109-110); the only duplicate carve-out in commit_fence covers FENCED-current vs OPEN-incoming (lines 101-107), not an OPEN retry. verified_findings.failure_scenario: Two different attempts whose components merely shift an underscore boundary — e.g. (module_run_id="run_a", variant_id="b", attempt_id="c1x", "result") and (module_run_id="run", variant_id="a_b", attempt_id="c1x", "result") — both produce idempotency key "run_a_b_c1x_result"; put_bytes then finds the prior artifact under that key with different content and raises ValueError("Cell artifact idempotency conflict"), so the second attempt's successfully generated provider output is discarded and the attempt is recorded as failed even though nothing actually conflicted.
verified_findings.summary: commit_output (and commit_failure_detail at line 239) builds the artifact idempotency key by underscore-joining module_run_id, variant_id, attempt_id, and logical_name, but the runtime ID grammar ([a-z][a-z0-9_.-]{2,159}) allows underscores inside each component, so distinct lineage tuples can join to the identical key — the ambiguous-delimiter pitfall the file's own _stable_id avoids with "\x1f" joins.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: A Workflow Release with a waiting review node whose 'approved' outcome edge is terminal=True (target_node_id None) is registered and admitted; when the Product Gateway submits the authorized approval event, prepare_ingress raises PermissionError('external event has no unique nonterminal graph edge'). The execution stays in 'waiting' forever — the human approval that should finish the workflow is rejected, while the durability layer's graph projection would have accepted the same transition to its 'completed' terminal state.
verified_findings.summary: prepare_ingress rejects any requested event whose unique workflow edge is terminal (target_node_id is None), so an authorized external decision can never complete a waiting execution, even though project_workflow_release_graph supports terminal transitions via the 'completed' control state.

verification_history.evidence: execution_event_ingestion.py:640-641 reads `if len(routes) != 1 or routes[0].target_node_id is None: raise PermissionError("external event has no unique nonterminal graph edge")` — a unique matching edge that is terminal is rejected. verified_findings.failure_scenario: A Product Gateway submits an authorized external event, the response is lost to a network failure, and it retries prepare_ingress with the exact same ExternalEventIngressRequest and evidence but a fresh claim_at_utc (current time). The rebuilt record differs only in recorded_at_utc, so `existing != record` and the call raises ValueError 'external-event ingress idempotency conflict'; the retry path can never claim the wait even though apply() is written to be retry-safe, permanently stalling the waiting workflow transition for that request.
verified_findings.summary: prepare_ingress bakes the caller-supplied claim_at_utc into the ingress record (recorded_at_utc, hashed into ingress_record_sha256) and then requires full equality with the stored record for idempotent replay, so any retry of the identical request at a later timestamp raises instead of returning the committed record.

verification_history.evidence: src/agent_runtime/execution/execution_event_ingestion.py builds the ingress record with the caller clock — line 681 `recorded_at_utc=claim_at_utc,` — and `ExternalEventIngressRecord._payload()` includes `"recorded_at_utc": self.recorded_at_utc` (line 408) which `build()` hashes into `ingress_record_sha256` (lines 428-434). Replay then demands whole-record equality: lines 683-687 `existing = self._ingress_by_request.get(request.request_ref)` / `if existing is not None: if existing != record: raise ValueError("external-event ingress idempotency conflict")`. Since `ExternalEvent` has no timestamp field and both `_stable_id` calls (lines 642-647, 672-676) exclude claim_at_utc, an identical retry with a fresh claim_at_utc (still within the validity window checked at lines 871-880) rebuilds a record differing only in recorded_at_utc/ingress_record_sha256; the frozen-dataclass `!=` is true and prepare_ingress raises instead of returning the committed record. By contrast `apply()` is timestamp-insensitive (lines 733-735 return `existing` by event_ref with no equality check). This contradicts designDoc/agent_runtime_03_authorized_external_event_ingress.md section 4 ("One logical external action keeps the same ... ingress record across transport retries") and its failure-contract row "Ingress already committed with identical content | Return or continue the original lineage". The only replay test passes the identical hardcoded timestamp (tests/test_agent_runtime_external_event_ingress.py line 318 `claim_at_utc=NOW`), so the fresh-timestamp retry path is untested.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator bug passes the correct prepare-time token together with an ExecutionSnapshot from a different (or outdated) execution that happens to be in the same waiting domain state: every check in apply() passes (token matches event expectations; the foreign snapshot matches expected_domain_state and 'waiting'), so an ExternalEventApplicationRecord is committed asserting the target execution's wait was atomically revalidated when it was not — corrupting the sole authoritative application evidence that downstream acknowledge() then binds into the ledger.
verified_findings.summary: apply() validates the snapshot token against the event's expectations and the snapshot's domain_state/runtime_status separately, but unlike prepare_ingress it never cross-checks that current_snapshot and current_snapshot_token describe the same snapshot (token.domain_state_id/runtime_status_id/workflow_execution_id vs the snapshot's fields).

verification_history.evidence: apply() at execution_event_ingestion.py:708-717 checks only `current_snapshot_token.snapshot_ref != event.expected_snapshot_ref or current_snapshot_token.snapshot_sha256 != event.expected_snapshot_sha256 or current_snapshot_token.transition_sequence != event.expected_transition_sequence or current_snapshot.domain_state_id != event.expected_domain_state or current_snapshot.runtime_status_id != "waiting"` — token fields are compared to the event and snapshot fields to the event, but token and snapshot are never compared to each other (no domain_state_id/runtime_status_id/workflow_execution_id/transition_sequence cross-check), and current_snapshot.workflow_execution_id is never compared to event.workflow_execution_id. The prepare path proves this binding is intended: _validate_prepare_closure enforces `snapshot_token.domain_state_id != snapshot.domain_state_id or snapshot_token.runtime_status_id != snapshot.runtime_status_id` (lines 867-868) and `request.workflow_execution_id != snapshot.workflow_execution_id or request.workflow_execution_id != snapshot_token.workflow_execution_id` (lines 815-816). The per-object validate() calls at lines 703-704 don't close the gap: ExecutionSnapshotToken.validate() hashes only the token's own payload (lines 124-125: `if self.snapshot_sha256 != _canonical_sha256(self._payload())`), and ExecutionSnapshot.validate() (durability_backend_definition.py:180-211) checks field formats only. Concrete trigger: call apply() with the valid ingress record, the correct prepare-time token, and an ExecutionSnapshot from a different execution (different workflow_execution_id and/or transition_sequence) whose domain_state_id equals event.expected_domain_state and runtime_status_id == "waiting" — all checks pass and lines 741-762 commit an ExternalEventApplicationRecord with disposition APPLIED (class docstring line 439: "Sole Runtime evidence that one waiting transition was applied") whose pre_application_* fields are taken solely from the token (lines 747-753), so the foreign snapshot leaves no trace and acknowledge() then binds the false evidence into the acknowledgement lineage. No other in-repo caller adds the check (only tests call apply()), and per the module docstring (lines 3-5) this in-memory implementation is the conformance contract production adapters must mirror.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Five modules own the runtime ID derivation independently; changing the separator, digest length, or prefix grammar in one place produces IDs that collide with or fail cross-module lookups against IDs minted by the others, and none of the copies enforce the prefix grammar the public helper validates.
verified_findings.summary: _stable_id is the fifth identical private copy (also execution_event_ingestion.py:51, execution_content_staging.py:31, execution_operation_authorization.py:29, execution_authorization_coordination.py:37) of the public stable_runtime_id helper in contracts/ledger_record_definition.py:54, minus its prefix validation

verification_history.evidence: All five private copies are byte-identical: execution_module_invocation.py:59-61, execution_event_ingestion.py:51-53, execution_content_staging.py:31-33, execution_operation_authorization.py:29-31, and execution_authorization_coordination.py:37-39 each read exactly `def _stable_id(prefix: str, *parts: str) -> str: digest = hashlib.sha256("\x1f".join(parts).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:24]; return f"{prefix}_{digest}"`. The public helper contracts/ledger_record_definition.py:54-61 computes the same derivation (`digest = hashlib.sha256("\x1f".join(parts).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()` then `return f"{clean_prefix}_{digest[:24]}"`) but adds prefix normalization and grammar validation the copies omit: `clean_prefix = str(prefix).strip().lower()` and `if not re.fullmatch(r"[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,30}", clean_prefix): raise ValueError(f"invalid runtime id prefix: {prefix!r}")`. The helper is public (`"stable_runtime_id"` in __all__ at ledger_record_definition.py:3272) and mints ledger-surface IDs (ledger_record_persistence.py:335 `transaction_id=stable_runtime_id(...)`), while the execution surface mints its IDs through the five private copies (e.g. execution_module_invocation.py:157 `module_run_id = _stable_id("module_run", ...)`, execution_event_ingestion.py:642 `event_id = _stable_id(...)`), so the same ID grammar is owned in six places and none of the five copies enforce the prefix rule — a divergent edit to separator, digest length, or prefix handling in any one copy silently changes that module's IDs relative to the others.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Timestamps minted by different execution modules have different precision, and this module's _as_datetime slices value[:-1] off arbitrary strings without validating — a malformed expiry string raises a bare ValueError from fromisoformat with no field label instead of the typed 'invalid …: UTC timestamp required' error every other module produces, making authority-window failures inconsistent to debug. One shared clock/parse helper removes the drift.
verified_findings.summary: _utc_now and _as_datetime are copy-pasted across three execution modules (also execution_authorization_coordination.py:28/32, execution_module_invocation.py:80, execution_event_ingestion.py:56) with drift: this module's _as_datetime skips validation entirely and execution_module_invocation's _utc_now adds a microseconds timespec

verification_history.evidence: Duplication and both drift claims are exact. execution_operation_authorization.py:25-26 `_utc_now` = `datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat().replace("+00:00", "Z")` and :34-35 `_as_datetime` = `return datetime.fromisoformat(value[:-1] + "+00:00")` with no validation; execution_authorization_coordination.py:28-34 repeats `_utc_now` but its `_as_datetime` first calls `validate_utc_timestamp("observed_at_utc", value)`; execution_event_ingestion.py:56-58 repeats `_as_datetime` with `validate_utc_timestamp("timestamp", value)`; execution_module_invocation.py:80-83 repeats `_utc_now` as `isoformat(timespec="microseconds")`. verified_findings.failure_scenario: A Module whose output schema declares a property named "anyOf" or "if" runs with output_constraint_mode native_structured_output: ClaudeAgentOptions.output_format receives a schema without that property, the provider constrains the response to the corrupted shape, and the committed output then fails validation against the full registered schema at line 636 (required property missing), so every Attempt of that Module fails as output_validation_failure.

verification_history.evidence: invocation_claude_module_invocation.py:418-422 performs an order-sensitive tuple comparison: `declared_names = tuple(definition.tool_name for definition in definitions)` then `if declared_names != profile.tool_policy: raise PermissionError("Gateway tool session differs from the selected Execution Profile")`. verified_findings.failure_scenario: A long-running host accumulates one directory per attempt forever (unbounded disk growth under workspace_root), and any re-execution of the same attempt_id after a crash fails on the leftover directory — Claude converts it to a non-retryable workspace_initialization_failure, permanently blocking that attempt's replay even though nothing durable was committed.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: Every successful attempt pays an extra full parse of the output payload (and the Codex path an extra serialize besides) purely because the intermediate object is discarded; for large structured outputs this doubles the post-provider CPU work on the invocation hot path. Keeping the parsed payload and serializing once at commit does the same job.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: On a host running under LANG=C/POSIX (typical minimal containers, systemd units, CI runners), any Prompt Envelope containing a non-ASCII character — routine, since prompts embed user text and ensure_ascii=False JSON — makes subprocess.run raise UnicodeEncodeError before the CLI runs; the except block at line 416 records it as failure_code codex_cli_invocation_error with failure_class provider_failure, which _failure_detail_bytes marks retryable=true, so a deterministic local misconfiguration is retried indefinitely as a transient provider failure (non-ASCII CLI stdout similarly fails decoding after a successful run).
verified_findings.summary: _default_invoke calls subprocess.run(argv, input=prompt, text=True, ...) without encoding="utf-8", so prompt encoding and stdout/stderr decoding use locale.getpreferredencoding(), unlike every other byte boundary in the adapters which pins UTF-8 (prompt bytes are validated as exact UTF-8 at line 318-321 before being handed to the locale-dependent pipe).

verification_history.evidence: Code facts verified: lines 82-90 read `subprocess.run(argv, input=prompt, capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=str(cwd), timeout=timeout_seconds, check=False)` — no `encoding=` — so encode/decode uses locale.getpreferredencoding(False); line 319 pins the prompt as UTF-8 (`prompt = prompt_bytes.decode("utf-8")`) and every other byte boundary in both adapters pins utf-8 (lines 169, 182, 193, 200, 407, 484, 493; claude adapter 191, 239, 249, 258, 399), making line 82 the sole unpinned boundary. The consequence chain is confirmed: `except Exception` at 416 maps non-TimeoutExpired to failure_class "provider_failure"/failure_code "codex_cli_invocation_error" (419-428), and _raise_failure sets `retryable=failure_class in {"provider_failure", "provider_timeout"}` (544-547) → retryable=true for a deterministic local encoding error. I reproduced the exact crash with the same call shape: under LC_ALL=en_US.ISO8859-1, `subprocess.run(['cat'], input='ok → done', text=True, ...)` raises `UnicodeEncodeError: 'latin-1' codec can't encode character '→'`, and under LANG=C PYTHONUTF8=0 PYTHONCOERCECLOCALE=0 it raises `'ascii' codec can't encode character '\xe9'`. However, the candidate's headline trigger is wrong: on the repo's required CPython (pyproject line 10: requires-python ">=3.11"), LANG=C/POSIX auto-enables UTF-8 mode (PEP 540) — measured `env -i LANG=C python3` → `utf8_mode: 1 preferred: UTF-8` (same for LC_ALL=C) and the call succeeds with non-ASCII input, so "typical minimal containers, systemd units, CI runners" running under C locale are NOT affected. verified_findings.summary: Module-level 'from temporalio.api.history.v1 import History' has no importorskip guard, so pytest collection errors (not skips) in any environment without the optional temporal extra.

verification_history.evidence: tests/test_agent_runtime_temporal_integration.py:13-15 imports temporalio unconditionally at module top level: `from temporalio.api.history.v1 import History`, `from temporalio.testing import WorkflowEnvironment`, `from temporalio.worker import Replayer, Worker` — no importorskip exists anywhere in tests/ (grep found only one `@pytest.mark.skipif` at line 294, `os.environ.get("RUN_TEMPORAL_INTEGRATION") != "1"`, a decorator evaluated only after module import succeeds). pyproject.toml makes temporalio optional: base `dependencies = ["jsonschema>=4.23"]`, with `temporal = ["temporalio>=1.31"]` only under [project.optional-dependencies], and the `test` extra (`pytest>=8`) does not include it. `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` sets `testpaths = ["tests"]` with no addopts, and no conftest.py exists in the repo, so `python -m pytest` always collects this file. Trigger: install agent-runtime-core (with or without [test]) but without [temporal], run pytest — collection imports the module, line 13 raises ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'temporalio', pytest reports 'ERROR collecting tests/test_agent_runtime_temporal_integration.py' and exits non-zero rather than skipping. The transitive import at lines 17-24 hits the same wall: src/agent_runtime/testing/durability_temporal_conformance.py line 20 does `from temporalio import activity, workflow` at module level. The claim's framing that other tests survive without extras also holds: grep shows no other test file imports temporalio/claude_agent_sdk/psycopg at module level (only string references), so this is the sole file that hard-fails collection.

verified_findings.failure_scenario: A wheel consumer opens the installed agent_runtime/design_contract/the_agent_runtime.md and follows the [agent_runtime_10] link for the workflow-execution-binding-and-admission contract (also listed as a related contract by packaged contracts 00 and 08); the file is missing from the installed package, so the admission/binding terms that the packaged contracts declare as governing related behavior are unreadable from the shipped artifact and the bundle's own index misrepresents its contents.
verified_findings.summary: CANONICAL_DOCUMENTS excludes contracts 02, 05, and 10 from the packaged Design Contract bundle, but the bundle still ships documents that reference them 13 times, including relative markdown links in the packaged the_agent_runtime.md contract-index table ([agent_runtime_02], [agent_runtime_05], [agent_runtime_10]) that resolve inside design_contract/ where the files do not exist.

verification_history.evidence: tools/build_agent_runtime_design_contract_bundle.py:21-31 defines CANONICAL_DOCUMENTS containing only the_agent_runtime.md and contracts 00, 01, 03, 04, 06, 07, 08, 09 — 02, 05, and 10 are excluded — and ls of src/agent_runtime/design_contract/ confirms those three .md files are absent while pyproject.toml:39 ('"agent_runtime" = ["README.md", "design_contract/*.md", "design_contract/*.json"]') ships the bundle in the wheel. The packaged bundle references the excluded contracts on 18 lines (22 occurrences — the claimed 13 is understated), including dead relative links in the packaged the_agent_runtime.md contract-index table that resolve inside design_contract/: line 631 '| [agent_runtime_02](agent_runtime_02_product_target_topology.md) |', line 634 '| [agent_runtime_05](agent_runtime_05_delivery_roadmap.md) |', line 639 '| [agent_runtime_10](agent_runtime_10_workflow_execution_binding_and_admission_contract.md) |'. The failure scenario's supporting claim also holds: packaged agent_runtime_00_execution_charter.md lines 49 and 60 list 'designDoc/agent_runtime_10_workflow_execution_binding_and_admission_contract.md' as a related contract, and packaged agent_runtime_08_agent_execution_adapter_contract.md:831 is itself a dead relative link '[`agent_runtime_10_workflow_execution_binding_and_admission_contract.md`](agent_runtime_10_workflow_execution_binding_and_admission_contract.md)'. Trigger: a wheel consumer opens installed agent_runtime/design_contract/the_agent_runtime.md and follows the [agent_runtime_10] index link → the target file does not exist in the installed package, so the bundle's own index misrepresents its contents.
